content:
Earlier this year, I swapped out a battery-powered push mower for a robot mower controlled by an iPhone. That unit builds a virtual map by letting you manually drive it around the perimeter of your yard. Once set up, it automatically handles mowing on a schedule.

Recently, I've been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It takes a completely different approach to navigation, and after several weeks of testing, I think it might be the easier choice for a lot of people.

Camera-driven automatic map building

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier comes down to how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning, and setup required me to manually drive the mower around the perimeter from an iPhone to build the initial map.

The TerraMow V1000 uses what the company calls TerraVision 2.0. With three cameras, the mower can automatically map your lawn and navigate without needing buried boundary wire or a separate RTK antenna.

The automatic method of building my initial map definitely took longer, but I think it could be easier for someone less inclined to tinker with technology.

To test that idea, I had my mom in another state (meaning a different U.S. state) set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own, with no help from me. She reported that it worked well. But I'm not sure she would have had the patience to manually drive a robot around the entire perimeter and manually flag zones to avoid.

Automatic map building did introduce one small quirk in my front yard. There's no fence or other physical separation between my lawn and my neighbor's, so TerraMow initially added part of their yard to my map.

I fixed it by marking that area as a no-go zone in the app. However, lawns without a clear visual boundary may require extra attention during the initial map-building process.

A look through the mower's camera

The cameras on TerraMow also enable one of my favorite features. The iPhone app lets you see in real time what the mower sees as it works.

During testing, I used iPhone Mirroring on my Mac to keep that feed open in a large window. I could work inside while watching, from the mower's perspective, as it moved around the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automated mowing, but it makes the robot more fun and occasionally helps explain why it slows down or avoids something. The Anthbot M9 doesn't offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps are similar in many ways, letting you schedule work, adjust mowing behavior, build zones, flag areas to avoid, and remotely drive the mower.

TerraMow has one particularly nice twist on that last feature. In addition to the usual left/right virtual joysticks, its app offers a single-hand joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone naturally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower from an iPhone isn't the primary use case for either system; ideally, the robot should just run on its schedule with no input. Still, TerraMow's joystick is pretty delightful for tidying up missed patches.

Sometimes it almost felt like I was controlling the robot with my thoughts (in a good way). I could hold the iPhone at my side, walk alongside the mower, and direct it with barely a thumb twitch.

Every robot mower app should copy this control scheme.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut lower and was louder while working.

I wouldn't call TerraMow noisy, but the difference is noticeable. The Anthbot runs so quietly it's easy to forget it's operating, including when it mows after sunset using its headlights.

Since TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably, so daytime scheduling matters more.

The V1000 also feels solid and is physically larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage over the charging dock, while Anthbot's garage is sold separately.

Most importantly, TerraMow has been reliable. I've used it for weeks on end without ever needing to take over the daily mowing myself.

When adaptive maps get too clever

The same visual smarts that make TerraMow easy to set up occasionally work against it.

The mower continually adjusts its map based on what it sees. Saving those adjustments after each run takes a long time, during which you can't do other things in the app.

After several straight days of rain, I ran into an interesting edge case. Part of the yard pooled with water, and TerraMow sensibly avoided that area during its next run.

Within the skipped circular patch, the grass then grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to treat that growth as something to keep avoiding, even after the ground had dried out, and the area never got cut.

I ultimately fixed it by using the app's remote control to manually drive the mower through the taller patch. Once that area looked like lawn again, automated mowing resumed there as normal.

Regular trimming along the edges also helps TerraMow reliably reach the boundary. Tall grass growing along an unclear edge can otherwise be mistaken for an obstacle instead of part of the mowing area.

Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles you define yourself, which takes more effort up front but avoids the map "changing its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac Opinion

Having used both systems, I think TerraMow's camera-based approach is the better fit for most people.

For me, burying boundary wire is a non-starter, and installing an RTK base station means one more piece of hardware to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow avoids both requirements.

Its vision-based navigation isn't flawless: the initial map takes longer to build, one invisible property line needed manual correction, and its adaptive behavior once mistook a patch of tall grass for a permanent obstacle.

All of those issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automated mowing, an engaging live camera view, and the best manual controls I've used in a robot mower app.

I genuinely enjoy working in the yard, but mowing is the repetitive, tedious part. Handing it off to a robot frees me up to focus on landscaping, edging, and detail work while keeping the lawn looking sharp.

The TerraMow V1000 delivers well enough on that to earn my recommendation, especially for anyone who wants to avoid burying wire, setting up an RTK antenna, or manually driving through the entire yard from an iPhone.

Amazon currently has the TerraMow V1000 listed at $999, with a $200 coupon available on the site that brings the price down. You can also find it on TerraMow's website.
